Jonathan Swift. Born in sixteen sixty-seven and dying in seventeen forty-five, Swift was an Irish author and satirist whose savage wit and misanthropic vision made him one of the defining literary voices of the Enlightenment.

Born in Dublin but educated and living much of his life in England, his Irishness gave him a perspective of outsider-within on English politics and society. Through Gulliver's Travels, his masterpiece, Swift deployed ironic rage to expose the follies and cruelties of his age. Framed as a voyage narrative, the work functions as a systematic satire of human nature, politics, and the conceits of empirical science itself.

A Modest Proposal, published in seventeen twenty-nine, is his most famous essay: a deadpan suggestion that the Irish solve famine by selling their children as food to the English. The irony exposes English indifference to Irish suffering with devastating clarity. Swift's irony is so complete and sustained that readers sometimes miss the moral outrage beneath it. His satire operates on the principle of letting the reader discover the horror themselves.

His later years brought increasing anger and isolation. Works like A Tale of a Tub grow more obscure and vicious in their attack on human presumption. Swift suffered from mental illness and was diagnosed with dementia late in life, famously writing that he would die like a poisoned rat in a hole. Yet he left much of his estate to found a mental hospital in Dublin, a gift befitting a writer obsessed with human folly and breakdown.
